amendments.rule:
**An anarthrous substantive takes the English the ASV supplies to make it one.** A participle or adjective used as a noun with no article morpheme present still needs an English noun phrase, and the ASV supplies it: a bare *the*, or a pronoun with a relative — *him that*, *them that*, *they that*, *those that*. No article is present to take that English and nothing else licenses it, so it joins the substantive's own unit and is never `added`. `זֵדִים` → *the proud*, `צַדִּיק` → *the righteous*, `יִרְאֵי יְהוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah*, `עֹשְׁקֵי` → *those that oppress*, `עֹבֵד` → *him that serveth*. **Head on the word carrying the lexeme**, by rule 31's subtraction: *proud*, *righteous*, *feared*, *oppress*, *serveth*. This does not contradict rule 41's heading on the pronoun. There the supplied pronoun is the whole of what the article is rendered by, so it is the only candidate; here the substantive's own lexeme sits in the same unit and outranks a word the ASV supplied. Read whether an article morpheme is present, and let that decide which rule governs. Two riders. Where the Hebrew supplies a relative of its own, that relative takes the *that* and the supplied antecedent goes with it — `לַאֲשֶׁר לֹא עֲבָדוֹ` → *him that serveth him not* puts *him that* on `אֲשֶׁר` — since a present morpheme takes its English before a bare participle does. And where the ASV writes the antecedent once across coordinated substantives, the later ones take only what is written: `וְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ` → *and that thought upon his name* leaves the participle *that thought upon*, under rule 22.

**A headless relative clause is read the same way, and its verb may be finite.** Where the Hebrew writes a relative clause with no antecedent noun and no `אֲשֶׁר`, the whole clause stands in a nominal slot and the ASV must supply a noun phrase for it: `אַחֲרֵי לֹא יוֹעִלוּ הָלָכוּ` → *walked after* ***things that do*** *not* ***profit***, `בְּלוֹא יוֹעִיל` → *for* ***that which doth*** *not* ***profit***. The supplied antecedent and relative join the clause's own unit and head on the word carrying the lexeme, exactly as *them that* joins a bare participle above and for the same reason: no article and no relative morpheme is present to take them, and nothing else licenses them, so neither is `added`. The unit is discontinuous around the negative or any other intervening word under rule 25, and a Hebrew noun the ASV recasts the same way — `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* — goes with it. **This governs only a clause with no antecedent of its own.** Where the Hebrew writes the antecedent and the ASV supplies a relative for a finite clause juxtaposed to it, nothing in this rule licenses that word: it subordinates a clause rather than making one a noun, and rules 30 and 55 are what decide it. Rule 41's articleless attributive is a third case again, and is decided there.
amendments.why: Rule 46 as it stands covers 'a participle or adjective used as a noun', and says nothing about a headless relative clause whose verb is finite. JER.2.8 (אַחֲרֵי לֹא יוֹעִלוּ -> 'after things that do not profit') and JER.2.11 (בְּלוֹא יוֹעִיל -> 'for that which doth not profit') are exactly that construction, and both verses placed the supplied antecedent and relative on the verb by rule 46's own reasoning, with JER.2.37's recast noun מִבְטַחַיִךְ -> 'those in whom thou trustest' following. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so that the 'participle or adjective' sentence is not left standing as the whole of the case, which is what would invite either an added antecedent or a stray unit. Nothing in the corpus tables supplied contradicts it: the הַ table's 238 'that' units are article morphemes taking a written relative, a different construction. The closing boundary sentence is deliberately narrow — it puts a supplied relative for a clause with a written antecedent out of this rule's scope and hands it to rules 30 and 55 rather than asserting an outcome, because JER.2.6 has a resumptive בָּהּ in the clause and JER.2.24 has nothing, and rule 30's subtraction is the right place to settle whether a morpheme answers to the word.

conventions: A relative the ASV supplies where the Hebrew writes none is placed three ways in this chapter, and what the source writes decides which. An articleless attributive takes it with its own English and any copula: אֶרֶץ לֹא זְרוּעָה -> 'a land that was not sown' (2.2, rule 41). A headless clause takes it together with the supplied antecedent, headed on the verb: לֹא יוֹעִלוּ -> 'things that do not profit' (2.8), לוֹא יוֹעִיל -> 'that which doth not profit' (2.11), and the noun מִבְטַחַיִךְ recast as 'those in whom thou trustest' (2.37), all on rule 46's reasoning. But a finite clause merely juxtaposed to an explicit Hebrew noun licenses nothing, so the relative is added: 'a land that none passed through' (2.6), 'a wild ass that snuffeth up the wind' (2.24). A competing reading of 2.6 puts that 'that' on the resumptive suffix of בָּהּ, which 2.24 has no counterpart for; the chapter took added in both, and rule 55's instruction not to fold a supplied subordinator into a neighbouring rendering is why.

The interrogative particle (הֲ / הַ, tagged Ti) is unrepresented at all five occurrences: 2.11, 2.17, 2.31 and 2.32 mark the question by inversion alone, so the fronted auxiliary — 'Hath', 'Hast', 'Have', 'Can' — belongs to the verb it inflects under rule 17, and 2.14's 'Is' is the copula rule 20 gives the verbless clause's predicate. The particle would take English only where the ASV spends a word on the question itself, as the corpus's four הֲ -> 'should' units do. All five BSB disagreements tagged Ti follow from this and are convention differences. Promoting this would want a corpus query on LEMMA=הַ MORPH=Ti to show how the unrepresented majority is treated.

מִן compounded with a second particle and rendered by one English word is a single rule 30 unit headed on מִן: מִבְּלִי -> 'without' (2.15), מֵעַל -> 'from' (2.5), מֵאֵת -> 'From' (2.37). The last two were first aligned with מִן taking the word and the second preposition unrepresented, and were corrected in reconciliation. That a member's literal sense ('upon', 'with') is absorbed does not defeat fusion — rule 30's own בְּיַד -> 'by' and מִפְּנֵי -> 'because of' absorb theirs — while a second English word spent on one morpheme does, which is why מֵעוֹלָם -> 'of old time' (2.20) and בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת -> 'breaking in' (2.34) are split and בְּעֵת -> 'when' (2.17) is not.

Where an infinitive construct stands with no preposition before it and the ASV supplies a subordinator for the clause it heads, that word is added and is not folded onto the infinitive or its suffix: 'how' at 2.2, 'in that' as one unit at 2.17, 'that' at 2.19. Rules 48 and 52 hand a complementizer to a preposition that is actually present, and this chapter's 2.7 shows the counting rule at work in the other direction — two waws in the clause chain and two connectives written ('but', 'when'), so each waw takes one and nothing is added.

report: One real cross-verse split: מִן compounded with a second particle and rendered by a single English word is fused as one rule 30 unit in JER.2.15 (מִבְּלִי -> 'without') but split in JER.2.5 (מֵעַל -> 'from') and JER.2.37 (מֵאֵת -> 'From'), with the second preposition marked unrepresented. All three are contiguous compound prepositions with one English word written for the pair, so nothing in the source licenses the difference. Patched 2.5 and 2.37 to fuse, headed on the מִן that carries the ablative lexeme.

Rule 30 settles it on its own terms: it rejects 'one rendered morpheme beside others marked unrepresented' for a fixed expression rendered by one English word, and says a preposition before a construct noun fuses 'on the same terms as a compound preposition'. The corpus agrees: 26 units combine מֵ + אֵת into one unit (11 noncompositional 'from', 8 aligned 'from', 7 'of'), and 1CH.2.23 מֵ אִתָּה is the exact shape of 2.5's מֵעָלָי, the compound fused with the suffix as its own unit. Status aligned rather than noncompositional, matching this chapter's other rule 30 fusions (לְפָנַי, כַּאֲשֶׁר, לָמָּה, לָכֵן, בְּעֵת, כֻּלֹּה).

Checked and found licensed rather than split: the supplied relative, which the chapter places three ways (attributive in 2.2, headless in 2.8/2.11/2.37, asyndetic finite clause with a written antecedent in 2.6/2.24) with the source deciding each; the interrogative particle, unrepresented in all five occurrences; אֵת H853 against H854; the article הַ, which tracks whether the ASV writes a 'the' (2.2/2.6 have an article morpheme, 2.24 does not, hence its supplied 'the' on the construct); and rule 44's light-verb heads, which JER.2.3's own review note had already brought into line with 2.5.

The 13 added units are consistent in three families: a supplied subordinator before a bare infinitive construct (2.2 'how', 2.17 'in that', 2.19 'that' twice), a supplied connective in an asyndetic clause (2.15 'and', 2.20 'and', 2.32 'or'), and a supplied relative before an asyndetic finite clause with a written antecedent (2.6, 2.24). The remaining three (2.11 'its', 2.22 'thee', 2.23 'thou') are supplied possessives, objects and subject pronouns with no morpheme behind them, each contrasted in its own verse with a parallel that does have one.

BSB: 28 disagreements, none a genuine error. The four recurring families (R x 9, Td x 4, Ti x 5, and the object markers) are the documented convention differences named in rules 16, 27, 29 and 40. The singletons each follow a rule that names them: the resumptive suffix of בָּהּ in 2.6 and the אֲדֹנָי suffix in 2.19/2.22 under rule 22, אִם in 2.14 where the ASV writes no 'or', נַפְשָׁ in 2.24 where the ASV compresses 'the desire of her soul' to 'her desire', and the cohortative he of קוּמָה in 2.27 under rule 32. No accepted edge was changed to improve the aggregate.

The report's 60 repeated notes are per-unit rule citations ('Noun.', 'Suffix (rule 18).'), not chapter judgments; four judgments that a later reader would otherwise have to rediscover are recorded in the conventions log instead.

One amendment returned, to rule 46, extending it to a headless relative clause with a finite verb (2.8, 2.11), which its 'participle or adjective' sentence does not reach. No new rules. The chapter's treatment of the interrogative particle is left as a convention rather than promoted: the corpus's four הֲ -> 'should' units are compatible with it, but a corpus query on LEMMA=הַ MORPH=Ti is what would show whether the unrepresented majority agrees, and that is not worth spending the evidence round on while two corrections are ready to land.
